To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the compressibility of the medium stabilizes the Kelvin-Helmoltz instabilities for all modes propagating along the magnetic field, but that it destabilizes all other modes, and that the magnetic field stabilizes the Kelvin- Helmholtz instabilities only for modes propagating opposite to the flow direction.

the Kelvin-Helmholz instabilities are: (1) stabilized for (inverse plasma beta) > 1; (2) stabilized when the propagation angle is close to the flow direction; and (3) stabilized for the isothermal and mixed polytrope cases.

the compressibility of the plasma stabilizes the instability of a tangential velocity discontinuity, and the magnetic field can both stabilize and destabilize the instability, depending on the direction of the magnetic field and propagation angle.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the stability of a class of magnetohydrodynamic discontinuities.
the Kelvin-Helmoltz instabilities in high velocity magnetoplasma flows with isotropic or generalized anisotropic pressure laws.
the stability of magnetized plasms with generalized polytroptic equations of state.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Kelvin-Helmholz instability of magnetized velocity discontinuities is always present for modes at sufficiently general propagation angles and is always absent when the propagation angle is either parallel or antiparallel to the magnetic field.
for a given mode, the instability is enhanced by the compressibility and the magnetic field, and is reduced by the anisotropy in the pressure.
the Kelvin-Helmholz instability of tangentially sheared, magnetized plasms is strongly suppressed by both compressibility and magnetic field.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the compressibility, the magnetic field, and the pressure anisotropy all act to suppress the instability.
the compressibility and the anisotropy of the plasma pressure are stabilizing factors for the Kelvin-Helmhotz instability of the discontinuities.

, in the absence of the magnetic field, the instability is always present; in the presence of the magnetic field and for the case of isotropic pressure, the instability is present for all values of the plasma beta; and, in the presence of anisotropic pressure, the instability may be absent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the compressibility and the anisotropy of the pressure are stabilizing effects.
the Kelvin-Helmholz instability of magnetized, compressible flows is not a purely linear effect.
the Kelvin-Helmhotlz instabilities of tangential velocity jumps are more complicated than previously thought.
